title: Meng Reintroduces Diwali Day Act With 19 Co-Sponsors in the House
excerpt: Rep. Grace Meng brought back her bill to make Diwali the 12th US federal holiday a day after the festival, with five Indian-American lawmakers among the co-sponsors and 17 community organisations endorsing it.
body:
• Rep. Grace Meng reintroduced the Diwali Day Act in the House on November 9, a day after Diwali, proposing to make the festival a federal holiday.
  • The bill has 19 co-sponsors, including all five Indian-American House members: Ami Bera, Ro Khanna, Raja Krishnamoorthi, Suhas Subramanyam and Shri Thanedar.
  • If enacted, Diwali would become the 12th federally recognised holiday in the United States.
  • Nothing changes yet: the bill must still pass the House and Senate and be signed by the president, and Diwali 2026 fell on November 8, so any effect would come in a future year.

Rep. Grace Meng of New York, who chairs the Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus, reintroduced the Diwali Day Act on Monday, reviving her proposal to recognise Diwali as a federal holiday in the United States. The announcement came a day after communities across the country celebrated the festival.

Under the legislation, Diwali would become the 12th federally recognised holiday in the country. Meng is also the author of the Lunar New Year Day Act, a separate bill that would establish Lunar New Year as a federal holiday.

Who is backing the bill

The bill is co-sponsored by 19 members of Congress. Its supporters include the House's five Indian-American members — Reps. Ami Bera of California, Ro Khanna of California, Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois, Suhas Subramanyam of Virginia and Shri Thanedar of Michigan — alongside colleagues including Nanette Barragán, Wesley Bell, André Carson, Judy Chu, Suzan DelBene, Josh Gottheimer, Timothy Kennedy, Stephen Lynch, Deborah Ross, Lateefah Simon, Tom Suozzi, Mark Takano, Rashida Tlaib and Bonnie Watson Coleman.

Seventeen organisations have endorsed the bill, among them Asian Americans Advancing Justice, the Asian American Federation, the Coalition of Hindus of North America, Hindus for Human Rights, the Hindu Temple Society of North America, Indian American Impact, the Indian Diaspora Council, the Indo-Caribbean Alliance, the National Asian Pacific American Bar Association, the Sikh Coalition and the South Asian Impact Foundation.

"My Diwali Day Act is one step toward educating all Americans on the importance of this day, and celebrating the full face of American diversity."

— Rep. Grace Meng, introducing the bill's earlier version

A bill that has been here before

This is a reintroduction, not a first attempt. Meng first brought the Diwali Day Act to the House in May 2023, when it was referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Accountability as H.R. 3336 with 14 co-sponsors. Bills that do not pass before a Congress ends expire with it, which is why supporters have had to start the process again in the new session. The 19 co-sponsors on the new version are five more than the original drew.

States are moving faster than Washington

While the federal bill restarts its journey, state-level recognition has widened. California observed Diwali with a day off for the first time this year under a law that took effect on January 1, allowing public schools and community colleges to close and state employees to take the day; because Diwali fell on Sunday, November 8 this year, it was observed on Monday, November 9. New York City schools, Pennsylvania and Connecticut also recognise the festival. In February 2026, Washington state's Senate passed a bill recognising Diwali and Bandi Chhor Divas as state observances — a formal recognition, though not a paid legal holiday.

What a federal holiday would mean

A federal holiday closes federal offices and gives federal employees a paid day off. It does not require private employers or schools to close — those decisions stay with states, districts and employers — but it carries weight as an official statement that the day belongs on the national calendar. For Indian-American families, that recognition is the point of the campaign: a day on which celebrating together does not depend on using leave or seeking an excused absence.

What happens next

The bill now faces the same path as its predecessor: committee consideration in the House, passage by both chambers, and a presidential signature before it becomes law. No vote has been scheduled. Readers do not need to do anything at this stage — but anyone tracking it can watch for the bill's committee assignment and any hearing, which will be the first sign of whether this version moves further than the last.
